title: A cycle-based formulation and valid inequalities for DC power transmission problems with switching
contribution: Proves DC optimal transmission switching NP-complete even on series-parallel graphs with one source-sink pair (polynomial on trees), gives a KVL cycle formulation, the complete convex hull and facets of a single-cycle on/off relaxation with closed-form linear-time separation, and shows the cuts shrink trees, time and unsolved counts in CPLEX on released 118/300-bus instances.
problem_entry: Application complaint that lower-bounding for MILP switching models is 'largely ineffective' (Hedman et al. quote, p. 3) plus underdeveloped theory (abstract p. 1); goal stated as changing that reality with strong valid inequalities (p. 3).
key_idea: Replace angles by Kirchhoff's Voltage Law on a cycle basis, enforce it only when all arcs of a cycle are on, and convexify the single-cycle on/off set exactly via an all-on / at-least-one-off disjunction (pp. 5-7, 10-11).
assumptions: Connected network, one generator per bus WLOG, linear generation cost (flagged; convex-cost case argued but untested, p. 10), directed cycle and B_ij = 1 by scaling for the hull proof (pp. 4, 10-11).
proof_devices: Connected-optimal-solution lemma giving polynomiality on trees (Prop. 3.1, Cor. 3.1, p. 8)
Subset-sum reduction to a series-parallel two-terminal network with one generator and one load (Thm 3.1, pp. 8-9)
Two-term disjunction with integral sides, extended formulation (14) and its integrality (Prop. 4.1, pp. 11-12)
Projection of copied flows via hypercube-intersect-hyperplane feasibility (Prop. 4.2, pp. 12-14) then Fourier-Motzkin on the disjunction weight (pp. 14-15)
Facet proof by explicit affinely independent point families chi1-chi4, separate linear-independence argument when |C\S| = 1 (Thm 4.2, pp. 15-16)
Knapsack separation reduced to a closed-form threshold subset S*_C with necessary condition K_C > 0 (Props 4.3-4.4, pp. 17-18)
Cycle basis from LU decomposition of the edge-node incidence matrix with correctness proof (Algorithm 5, p. 21; Prop. A.1, pp. 30-32)
experiments: Five sets of 35 random instances derived from case118B and a modified case300 (released online), Default CPLEX vs BasicCycles vs MoreCycles cut-and-branch, single thread, 0.1% gap, 1 h; root gap closed, nodes, time, unsolved counts with arithmetic and geometric means and performance profiles; MoreCycles leaves 22 unsolved vs 43 for Default overall; callback variant 30% worse; reviewer-suggested switching-budget sensitivity study (pp. 19, 22-29).
positioning: Complexity established independently of and complementary to Lehmann et al. 2014 and extending Bienstock-Mattia 2007 (p. 8); inequalities placed in the IP tradition of cycle inequalities (Padberg, Barahona-Mahjoub, Ferreira et al., Van Vyve) (p. 4); DC model defended for planning against the Coffrin et al. critique (pp. 2-3).
writing: Four-bullet contribution list (p. 3); arbitrary choices and dead ends written plainly ('This choice of algorithm was arbitrary', p. 21; callbacks 30% worse, p. 19); reviewers credited for Section 6.3 and a future substructure (p. 30); moderate hedging ('promising', p. 1).
limits_future: Linear cost only, convex-cost bound strength untested (p. 10); substructure omits flow balance, so stronger extended formulations are possible (p. 30); future: other line addition/removal problems, richer substructures, larger networks (p. 30).

method_links.note: Exact convex hull, facets and separation for a recurring single-cycle on/off substructure, explicitly in the IP cycle-inequality tradition.
Complexity demarcated on both sides: trees polynomial, series-parallel with one source-sink pair NP-complete; every hull inequality shown facet-defining.

Cuts evaluated inside the full commercial solver (cut-and-branch with all features on) rather than a stripped instrument; callback version reported 30% worse. Instrument chosen for solver improvement, not explanation.
Lower bound is the stated target and root gap closed is the main yardstick, though the MIP is solved exactly rather than certifying a gap.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Optimal topologies switch off 42/85 lines on average against the 'few lines' literature; a cardinality-budget sweep with IP and LP values shows 11-15 lines capture nearly all benefit and explains harder budgeted MIPs.

transferable: Two-term 'all on / at least one off' disjunction for constraints active only when a whole set of binaries is 1; integral sides give an exact hull (pp. 11-12).
Fourier-Motzkin elimination of the single disjunction weight to read off an explicit facet-defining family (pp. 14-16).
Show that every positively contributing element is in an optimal separation set to turn a knapsack separation into a closed-form threshold rule (p. 18).
Report arithmetic and geometric means plus per-set performance profiles and say where the baseline wins (pp. 24-26).
coauthors: B. Kocuk (first author), H. Jeon, J. Linderoth, J. Luedtke, A. Sun

quotes.text: We prefer to implement our separation in this “cut-and-branch” manner in order to investigate the utility of the cutting planes when combined with all advanced features of modern MIP software.
We would like to thank the reviewers for their constructive comments and in particular suggesting the experiments in Section 6.3.

title: Relaxations and discretizations for the pooling problem
contribution: Unifies pooling formulations with full equivalence proofs, explains the strength of the pq-relaxation as the convex hull of single-pool sets and as a Lagrangian dual, proposes stronger RLT and Lagrangian relaxations, and tests flow/ratio discretization MILPs with valid inequalities, improving best known upper bounds on 6 of 70 instances.
problem_entry: Consolidation of a literature dispersed over optimization and chemical engineering plus refinery-driven need; MILP solver maturity motivates discretization (pp. 1-2, 18).
key_idea: Proportion variables live on a simplex, so level-1 RLT convexifies each single-pool bilinear set (Gupte's theorem), which explains PQ and points to enlarging the substructure; discretize one factor of each bilinear term to obtain MILP restrictions strengthened by knapsack facets lifted through the simplex theorem (pp. 11-13, 15, 18-20).
assumptions: Acyclic network, linear blending, spec values in [0,1], nontriviality observations; integer capacities for flow discretization and no principled choice of ratio grid n (pp. 3-5, 19).
proof_devices: Path-flow decomposition proof of equivalence of P, Q, PQ, HYB for generalized pooling (Prop. 2, pp. 7-8)
Sum-decomposition rule: single-term McCormick is optimal over bounds alone (Prop. 3, p. 12)
Simplex level-1 RLT convex hull theorem (Gupte) giving conv(Q_l) and PQ dominates P via the linear map q to p (Thm 1, p. 11; Prop. 4, p. 13)
DC-decomposition relaxation shown no stronger than envelopes because convex envelopes do not sum-decompose (Remark 2, p. 11)
Value function phi(q) plus saddle-point interchange: z_LAG1 = z_pq (Prop. 6, pp. 16-17); ordering (31) of LAG2, LAG3, R3 (p. 17)
Exponential disjunctive LP representations to evaluate Lagrangian bounds exactly on small instances (p. 21)
Superincreasing-knapsack cover facets and Marcotte divisible-knapsack rounding lifted by the simplex RLT theorem (Props 7-8, pp. 19-20)
experiments: Classic small instances used only for Lagrangian tests because BARON solves them in seconds; 70 random standard (Alfaki-Haugland, Dey-Gupte) and 10 generalized instances; BARON 6 h vs CPLEX 1 h with stated fairness rationale and aligned tolerances; LAG3 closes 12.5-100% of the gap on most small instances, R2 modest gains at high cost; discretization gaps vs BARON lower bound, performance profiles, time-to-best vs gap table; 6/70 improved upper bounds (pp. 20-25).
positioning: Extends prior pooling surveys and claims results stronger than Tawarmalani-Sahinidis and Alfaki-Haugland on PQ strength; reframes 'conventional wisdom' rather than attacking; SDP set aside for scalability (pp. 2, 7, 10, 13, 16).
writing: Three-part contribution statement (pp. 2-3); Observations/Remarks for easy facts; explicit 'We leave this idea open' (p. 15); flat negative findings (R1 no gain, R3 too large, p. 21); calibrated hedging ('seems to be a promising approach', p. 25).
limits_future: Strong Lagrangian bounds lack tractable formulations or separation (p. 25); no a priori rule to pick a discretization (p. 23); PQ discretizations too large for generalized instances (pp. 21, 23); future: dynamic discretization in branch-and-bound and solver tuning (pp. 20, 25).

method_links.note: Supplies the theorem behind the practitioner preference for the pq-formulation ('insight into the conventional wisdom'); the MILP-relaxation ratio theorem is only cited from Dey-Gupte.
PQ strength comes from jointly convexifying the single-pool substructure over a simplex; stronger relaxations come from enlarging the substructure (R2, R3).
New Lagrangian bounds computed exactly via exponential disjunctive LPs on small instances before any separation is engineered.
Dual bounds compared and gaps measured against BARON's lower bound, but the main deliverable is primal (MILP restrictions) and the strongest bounds are not tractable.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Survey of a dispersed literature with formal equivalence proofs (including one 'skipped in [4]') used as the platform for new relaxations and discretizations.

transferable: Use a simplex-domain RLT convex-hull theorem to see which partial-RLT inequalities are already implied and which enlargements can add strength (pp. 11-15).
Give the global solver a longer time limit than the MILP heuristic, state why, and align tolerances across solvers (p. 21).
Tabulate geometric-mean time-to-best-solution against geometric-mean gap per heuristic variant to separate fast-but-poor from slow-but-good (Table 6, p. 24).
Drop benchmark instances a global solver closes in seconds except for the experiment they still inform (p. 21).
coauthors: A. Gupte (first author), S. Ahmed, M.-S. Cheon (ExxonMobil)

quotes.text: Since these problems are solved in a matter of seconds by BARON, they are not of particular interest to us and are only used for demonstrating the strength of the Lagrangian relaxations in §5.1.
However, it is surprising that such a naive discretization gives fairly good solutions on random instances.

title: Mixed-integer quadratic programming is in NP
contribution: Proves that a feasible system with one (possibly nonconvex) quadratic inequality over a mixed-integer polyhedron has a polynomial-size solution, so decision MIQP is NP-complete, unifying QP in NP and ILP in NP, and shows tightness in the number of quadratic inequalities.
problem_entry: Gap at the join of two classical results (QP in NP, ILP in NP) stated as a small-certificate theorem; fixed-dimension IQP named as the open question beyond it (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Decompose the mixed-integer polyhedron into polytopes plus integer cones of simple cones, refine cones so zero-curvature faces have zero-curvature extreme rays, then analyse the quadratic one integer ray at a time and finish with Vavasis on the continuous part (pp. 3-9).
assumptions: Rational data, exactly one quadratic inequality with arbitrary symmetric H, linear constraints; pointedness obtained by orthant splitting (pp. 1, 6). Read from arXiv v1 (2014).
proof_devices: Simple-cone decomposition P_i + int.cone(R_K) via Caratheodory and fractional/integer splitting; MIP in NP as by-product (Props 4-5, pp. 3-5)
Normalizing hyperplane with polynomially bounded normal (Lemma 6, p. 5)
Inductive cone refinement around minimisers of the quadratic form (Lemma 7, pp. 5-6)
Negative recession curvature: explicit step from the larger root of a concave quadratic in lambda (Case 1, p. 7)
Linear-behaviour rays and norm bound via roots of a convex quadratic in lambda (Claims 1-2, pp. 7-9)
Tightness by three counterexamples: many quadratics undecidable, two quadratics (Pell) exponential, many convex quadratics exponential (pp. 2-3)
NP-hardness via max-cut as one quadratic inequality (Cor. 2, p. 2)
positioning: Presented as generalising and unifying Vavasis and the classical ILP-in-NP results; builds on Koeppe, Lagarias, Khachiyan for the negative examples and Del Pia-Weismantel as frontier; no criticism of prior work (pp. 1-3).
writing: Main theorem on p. 2 before preliminaries, immediately followed by a boundary paragraph of three negative results (pp. 2-3); named lemmas; proof of Lemma 7 framed as a constructive algorithm (p. 6); almost no hedging.
limits_future: Does not extend to two or many quadratics or many convex quadratics (pp. 2-3); the size polynomial is not made explicit (p. 2); open: IQP in fixed dimension (p. 1).

method_links.note: Boundary drawn hypothesis by hypothesis with three counterexamples; stated as tight in the number of quadratic inequalities.
Classical MILP small-solution / integer-cone decomposition carried into the quadratic class; the MILP question 'is it in NP?' asked of MIQP.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Chooses the class containing QP and ILP as special cases and proves the union, keeping both classical proofs as black boxes.

transferable: Write the boundary paragraph immediately after the main theorem, listing the nearest strengthenings with a known counterexample for each (pp. 2-3).
Reduce an unbounded mixed-integer region to finitely many polytope-plus-integer-simple-cone pieces so integrality becomes a product of Z_+ copies (pp. 3-4).
Use a normalizing hyperplane to turn cone-wide quadratic sign questions into compact QPs with small optimal solutions (pp. 5-6).

quotes.text: This result generalizes and unifies classical results that quadratic programming is in NP [11] and integer linear programming is in NP [1, 12, 4, 9].

The above examples serve to highlight the fact that the result of Theorem 1 (a feasible system of inequalities with exactly one quadratic inequality always has at least one integer feasible solution of small size) is tight with respect to the number of quadratic inequalities.

title: New formulation and strong MISOCP relaxations for AC optimal transmission switching problem
contribution: Gives an exact MINLP formulation of AC optimal transmission switching, a MISOCP relaxation strengthened by lifted arctangent envelopes, SDP- and McCormick-based cycle disjunctive cuts and neighbourhood bound tightening, and a two-phase algorithm that certifies small optimality gaps (0.05% IEEE, 1.16% NESTA congested averages) while finding large cost savings.
problem_entry: DC-based switching can be AC-infeasible and AC OTS is little explored (pp. 1-2); entry via the authors' own strong SOCP relaxations for OPF extended to switching (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Drop the nonconvex angle constraint from a MISOCP relaxation and reinject it through three cut families (lifted arctangent envelopes, SDP cycle disjunction, McCormick cycle disjunction) separated jointly, with tight bounds from local SOCPs and a solution-pool/no-good loop for primal topologies (pp. 6-14).
assumptions: Full AC rectangular model in (c, s) variables, c > 0 on boxes, linear or convex quadratic cost; finite convergence needs a global OPF oracle, otherwise only LB1 <= z* <= UB (pp. 3-7, 14).
proof_devices: Arctangent envelope planes through box corners shifted by max violation computed by KKT enumeration, lifted with (2pi - gamma')(1 - x) (Prop. 4.1, pp. 7-8)
Cycle disjunction 'all lines on' (SDP-representable) vs 'at least one off' (SOC-representable) (pp. 8-9)
Convex hull of union of two bounded conic sets via extended formulation (Appendix A, pp. 20-21)
Normalised conic separation problem from an extended conic set (Appendix B, p. 21)
Cycle angle condition as homogeneous polynomial bilinearised with artificial lines then McCormick (pp. 10-11)
experiments: 11 IEEE MATPOWER and 16 NESTA congested instances up to 300 buses (larger excluded because Phase II does not scale); nested settings SOCP, SOCPA, SOCPA Disj; metrics %OG, %CB, #off, total time on stated hardware with T1 = T2 = 5; QC-relaxation results of [18] compared from published numbers; gap attributed to integrality vs power-flow nonconvexity; hand-worked case6ww and best-line heuristic comparison (pp. 15-20).
positioning: Extends the authors' OPF work [27, 28] and the DC switching paper [29]; prior AC OTS approaches summarised neutrally; SDP tight but unwieldy at scale; DC criticised for AC infeasibility (pp. 2-3, 7, 15).
writing: Roadmap paragraph (pp. 2-3); abstract claims 'provably tight bounds' (p. 1); discussion section posed as two explicit questions (p. 18); hedged outlook ('We hope ...', p. 20).
limits_future: No scaling beyond 300 buses, MISOCP solve time is the bottleneck, some MISOCPs hit the time limit, global optimality needs a global OPF oracle (pp. 14, 16, 18, 20); future: faster MISOCPs, decomposition, stronger OPF relaxations (pp. 18, 20).

method_links.note: SOC-based relaxation (not SDP-first) strengthened by structure and paired with a local solver; proved %OG on stated hardware is the deliverable and the basis of the comparison with heuristics.
Cycle with on/off lines is the recurring substructure, convexified approximately through an all-on / at-least-one-off disjunction carried over from the DC paper.
Boundary stated computationally rather than by theorem: 300-bus limit, cases where the strongest method underperforms, oracle requirement for finite convergence.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: attribute the gap to its nonconvexity source
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Remaining optimality gap split between integrality and power-flow nonconvexity, using an instance where all topologies were enumerated so the gap is purely continuous.

transferable: Lift a continuous valid inequality to a switching model with a slack valid when the line is off, e.g. (2pi - gamma')(1 - x) (p. 8).
Tighten bounds and fix binaries with neighbourhood-restricted SOCPs (radius r = 2, solved in parallel) (pp. 12-13).
Use the MIP solution pool plus no-good cuts to enumerate candidate topologies and evaluate each with a local NLP, getting LB and UB from one loop (pp. 13-14).
coauthors: B. Kocuk (first author), X. A. Sun

quotes.text: Moreover, the best line heuristic does not provide any guarantee on how good the solution is while our algorithm gives optimality guarantees by construction.
Finally, we note that that optimality gaps can be explained by two non-convexities: 1) integrality, 2) power flow equations.

title: Bounding the gap between the McCormick relaxation and the convex hull for bilinear functions
contribution: Answers Luedtke-Namazifar-Linderoth's question negatively: the ratio of McCormick gap to convex-hull gap for bilinear functions on the hypercube is at least sqrt(n)/4 for almost all random +-1 instances and at most 600 sqrt(n) always, with an alternative proof of the Misener-Smadbeck-Floudas equality characterisation.
problem_entry: A named open question from a peer paper about a ratio measure of McCormick strength, motivated by McCormick's role in global solvers (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: At half-integral points the convex-hull gap equals half the range of cut weights in the fractional subgraph and the McCormick gap equals half the total absolute weight, turning the question into graph discrepancy of cuts (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: Bilinear functions with arbitrary real coefficients over [0,1]^n; random +-1 coefficients on the complete graph for the lower bound; explicit Hadamard instance (pp. 1-3, 7).
proof_devices: Envelope value as LP over vertex distributions with explicit primal (max cut) and dual certificate (Lemma 1, pp. 4-6)
Chernoff plus union bound over all cuts for the random lower bound (pp. 6-7)
Hadamard matrix with AM-GM for an explicit instance (Lemma 2, p. 7)
Random half-partition, Paley-Zygmund with Khintchine-Haagerup fourth moment, Cauchy-Schwarz, and a three-case argument for the cut discrepancy theorem (Thm 3, pp. 8-10)
Equality characterisation via quotient graphs of positive/negative paths (Thm 4, pp. 10-11)
positioning: Extends Luedtke-Namazifar-Linderoth and reuses their three-step skeleton with credit; Theorem 4 credited to Misener et al. and re-derived; thanks Nikolov and cites his Stack Exchange answer for the discrepancy argument (pp. 1-4, 10-12).
writing: All four theorems in a 'Main results' section before proofs, roadmap paragraph, Theorem 3 offered as 'of independent interest', crisp asymptotic-tightness phrasing, self-described as a note (pp. 1, 3-4).
limits_future: Constants 1/4 vs 600 far apart and not discussed; scope limited to bilinear functions on the hypercube; bipartiteness shown not to help with mixed signs (p. 11).

method_links.note: O(sqrt n) upper bound, matching lower bound for almost all instances plus an explicit construction, and exact characterisation of equality.
Analyses the default relaxation of spatial branch-and-bound solvers with a ratio measure fixed before the analysis.
Quantifies the cost of term-by-term McCormick versus convexifying the whole bilinear function, the quantitative case for joint convexification.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Takes the ratio and open question posed by Luedtke-Namazifar-Linderoth and settles it in both directions.

transferable: Evaluate convex/concave envelopes at half-integral points through the vertex-distribution LP and its dual to get a max-cut/min-cut formula (pp. 4-6).
Chernoff plus union bound over all cuts for random signed instances; Hadamard matrix for an explicit deterministic instance (pp. 6-7).
Paley-Zygmund with a Khintchine fourth-moment bound for constant-probability anti-concentration of a random signed sum (pp. 8-9).
Re-prove a known characterisation through your new correspondence to show its explanatory power, crediting the original (p. 10).
coauthors: N. Boland, T. Kalinowski, M. Molinaro, F. Rigterink

quotes.text: Answering a question of Luedtke, Namazifar and Linderoth, we show that this factor c cannot be bounded by a constant independent of n.
In order to prove Theorem 2 we establish the following discrepancy result which might be of independent interest.
